anchor: Whenever Richard Cory went down town
title: Richard Cory and Tilbury Town
short: Published in The Children of the Night (1897); one of Robinson's portraits of the people of 'Tilbury Town', modelled on Gardiner, Maine.
body: Robinson grew up in Gardiner, Maine, which became the 'Tilbury Town' of his poems; 'Richard Cory', 'Miniver Cheevy' and 'Mr. Flood's Party' belong to this gallery of small-town lives. The Children of the Night appeared from a small Boston press and was little noticed until Theodore Roosevelt praised it and recommended it to Scribner's, which issued a new edition in 1904. The 1890s were years of economic depression after the Panic of 1893, which also damaged the Robinson family's fortunes: this is the background to the townspeople's hardship in stanza 4. Paul Simon adapted the poem as a song recorded by Simon and Garfunkel on Sounds of Silence (1966).

sources.cite: Maine State Library, Maine Writers: Robinson, Edwin Arlington (1869-1935)
Scott Donaldson, Edwin Arlington Robinson: A Poet's Life (Columbia UP, 2007)

title: The collective speaker
short: The poem is spoken by 'we', the townsfolk on the pavement looking up at Cory; their envy shapes everything we see.
body: The speaker is plural and anonymous; we know Cory only as the crowd sees him. 'On the pavement' puts them literally on a lower level than the gentleman, and the phrase anticipates 'we... went without the meat'. The irony depends on this limited view: the town admires surfaces and never sees inside him. W. R. Robinson reads Tilbury Town as a place of spiritual shallowness in which appearances pass for reality.

sources.cite: W. R. Robinson, Edwin Arlington Robinson: A Poetry of the Act (Western Reserve UP, 1967)

title: 'from sole to crown'
short: From the soles of his feet to the top of his head, with a pun on a king's crown.
body: The phrase echoes the biblical 'from the sole of the foot even unto the head' (Isaiah 1:6) and, closer in wording, Job 2:7 ('from the sole of his foot unto his crown'). Closer in spirit is 2 Samuel 14:25, where Absalom is praised for beauty 'from the sole of the foot even to the crown of his head', a handsome prince who comes to a bad end. 'Crown' means the top of the head but also starts the royal vocabulary of 'imperially', 'arrayed' and 'richer than a king'. Some readers also hear 'sole' as 'soul', which would make the line claim more than the crowd can know.

title: 'Clean favored'
short: Having clean-cut, handsome features; 'favour' in the old sense of face or appearance.
body: The OED records 'favour' as an archaic word for the face or features, and 'favoured' with a qualifier ('well-favoured', 'ill-favoured', as of Pharaoh's cattle in Genesis 41) for someone's looks. 'Clean favored' thus means well-featured, neat and fine. The slightly old-fashioned compound suits the gentlemanly portrait. Every detail in the first stanza is physical and external: we learn how Cory looks, never what he thinks, which is precisely the limitation of the watching crowd and the ground of the final surprise.

title: 'imperially slim'
short: A surprising pairing: slimness becomes regal, the bearing of an emperor.
body: The adverb raises an ordinary physical trait to royal dignity, extending the 'crown' of line 3. Slimness also suggests a gentleman who does no heavy labour, set against the working townspeople. The phrase is among the most quoted in the poem because it captures the town's awe in two words, and the Gale commentary notes how it reinforces the speaker's view of Cory as a king.

title: 'quietly arrayed'
short: Dressed with understated elegance; 'arrayed' has biblical associations with royal clothing.
body: 'Arrayed' is the King James word for splendid dress: 'even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these' (Matthew 6:29). 'Quietly' tempers the splendour: Cory is tasteful, not showy. The Gale commentary reads the pairing as an oxymoron and notes that 'arrayed' can also mean drawn up in order, as for battle. Either way, clothing is part of the surface the town reads.

title: 'human when he talked'
short: He was kind and approachable in speech, a compliment that betrays how far above them he seemed.
body: To call a man 'human' when he talks implies that he might have been expected to be otherwise, a god or an aristocrat too grand to notice them. The townspeople are grateful for courtesy. The word is also ironic in retrospect: Cory's humanity, including his despair, is exactly what they never see. The adverb 'always', repeated in this stanza, stresses how unvarying the public performance was.

sources.cite: Scott Donaldson, Edwin Arlington Robinson: A Poet's Life (Columbia UP, 2007)

title: 'he glittered'
short: He shone like gold or a jewel; the image recalls the proverb that all that glitters is not gold.
body: The image makes Cory a precious object and hints at a gap between surface and substance, as in the proverb used in The Merchant of Venice (Act 2, scene 7, 'All that glisters is not gold'). The rhymes of the stanza (arrayed/said, talked/walked) are simple and conversational, so the striking verbs 'fluttered' and 'glittered' stand out. The townspeople's pulses 'flutter' at a simple greeting, a phrase more often used of romantic excitement, which measures the strength of their fascination.

sources.cite: Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 2 scene 7 (Folger Shakespeare)

title: Wealth and the American dream
short: The crowd's highest praise is money; the poem is often read as a critique of measuring happiness by wealth.
body: The dashes enclose an emphatic correction ('yes, richer than a king'), the voice of a speaker carried away by admiration. Richard P. Adams reads the poem as anti-materialist, and the Gale commentary describes it as an ironic comment on the American dream of wealth and success. Biographers note that Robinson watched his own family's fortune and his brothers' prospects collapse in the 1890s, which gave him a close view of what wealth could not protect.

sources.cite: Scott Donaldson, Edwin Arlington Robinson: A Poet's Life (Columbia UP, 2007)

title: 'schooled in every grace'
short: Educated in every social accomplishment; 'grace' also carries the religious sense the poem quietly withholds.
body: 'Graces' here means polite accomplishments, the manners of a gentleman. But in a poem that ends in despair after the townspeople's wait for 'the light', the theological sense of grace, the free gift of God that saves, is ironically absent from Cory's life. 'Schooled' implies something learned, not felt. The word thus points to the inner life that the poem never shows, and that the town never imagines.

title: 'In fine'
short: An old idiom meaning 'in short' or 'to sum up'.
body: The phrase was formal and slightly old-fashioned by the 1890s. Its point is sharp: the townspeople sum Cory up as 'everything', and their summary is about to be proved wrong. The third stanza closes the portrait with the confession of envy, 'To make us wish that we were in his place', the line the last stanza will turn inside out.

title: 'waited for the light'
short: Literally dawn and the start of work; figuratively a hope for better times or for spiritual revelation.
body: The phrase is deliberately open. It may mean that the workers rose before dawn, or that they waited for economic recovery after the depression of the 1890s, or that they waited for moral or religious illumination ('The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light', Isaiah 9:2). The title of the volume, The Children of the Night, frames human life as darkness awaiting light, and the Gale commentary surveys these readings.

sources.cite: Scott Donaldson, Edwin Arlington Robinson: A Poet's Life (Columbia UP, 2007)

title: Meat and bread
short: They could not afford meat and resented their plain bread: hardship set against Cory's wealth.
body: Meat stands for the luxury the poor went without, bread for the bare staple they had and did not value. The line also turns biblical language: the Lord's Prayer asks for 'daily bread' (Matthew 6:11), and Jesus answers the tempter that 'man shall not live by bread alone' (Matthew 4:4). The townspeople curse the bread they are given; Cory, who has everything material, lacks whatever else one lives by.

anchor: put a bullet through his head
title: The ending
short: The suicide is announced in the last line in the same calm voice; critics disagree about whether the twist is earned.
body: The form (four quatrains of iambic pentameter rhymed ABAB) and the flat 'one calm summer night' prepare nothing for the violence, which is the point. Yvor Winters judged the poem a neat portrait with a cheap surprise ending. Defenders argue that the details (the crowd's envy, the 'light' they wait for) prepare the reversal, and that the ending makes us reread the whole poem. Simon's 1966 song keeps the suicide but moves the weight to a new refrain, in which the singer still wishes he could be Richard Cory.

sources.cite: Yvor Winters, Edwin Arlington Robinson (New Directions, 1946)
